title: A wage floor can have modest overall employment effects while concentrating pressure on small chains
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35749, establishment-level evidence on California's AB 1228 fast-food minimum wage
geography: California fast-food establishments and chains covered or compared under the $20 hourly wage floor effective April 2024

observations.period: April 2024 policy implementation through the study's 2026 establishment-level analysis

denominator.unit: Fast-food establishments and chains in the study's establishment-level administrative data; exact public abstract denominator not disclosed

policy.unit: US dollars per hour for large fast-food chains under California AB 1228

employment_effect.value: negative employment effects, but modest overall effects thus far

small_chain_entry.value: policy slowed entry among small chains

small_chain_exit.value: policy increased exit among small chains

wage_worker_consumer_outcomes.value: not observed in the public abstract
wage_worker_consumer_outcomes.unit: missing worker earnings, hours, prices, product quality, customer demand, and household outcomes

observations.method: Establishment-level analysis designed to address chain-size coverage and industry-code measurement problems in aggregate datasets; the abstract reports a comparison of employment effects by chain size and entry/exit.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not disclose the establishment counts, full study window, effect sizes, or all specifications. This is a preliminary working paper; establishment entry or exit does not identify the same workers' wages, hours, or later employment.
observations.subgroup: Small chains and establishments covered by or exposed to California's fast-food wage floor; large chains receive separate treatment in the abstract, while individual workers, customers, franchise owners, and suppliers are not linked.
observations.counterinterpretation: Negative effects concentrated among small chains may reflect coverage, business composition, demand, labor substitution, or other adjustments rather than a single wage-cost mechanism. Modest overall employment effects can coexist with meaningful effects for particular workers or firms.

related_sources.claim: A separate NBER study using QCEW and QWI data reports different employment and separation-rate estimates, making measurement and unit choice part of the interpretation.
A separate NBER study estimates California fast-food price increases, supplying a consumer-price comparison rather than a worker or establishment outcome.

boundary: This record adds establishment-level evidence that small-chain entry and exit can move differently from aggregate employment after a wage-floor change. It does not establish worker earnings or hours, consumer prices, service quality, firm productivity, household welfare, or the policy's total causal effect.
